for bigamy was concluded to-day. The testimony
showed that the accused married Miss Emily
Florence MCGEE, of New York, in 1859; that he,
in the year 1861, married Miss Elizabeth Allan,
in London, and that the second marriage took

This state contains by estimate 95,634,240 acres of land, including submerged and swamp lands. Of the whole amount, about 60,900,900 will admit of cultivation; and there are 30,000,900 acres more which can be used for grazing purposes. Contrary to the general opinion, we have very little worthless land in this state. Much of it is mountainous or hilly; but not so valueless as to be undesirable for timber, grazing, wine growing, or other purposes. Counting the whole area which can be used in one way or another to contribute to the support of the population, we have 90,900,000 acres; of this amount hardly more than 2,000,000 acres are under cultivation, after reasonable allowance for the increased occupation and culture of the present year. It does not follow, of course, that all the rest can be had for the asking or is now in the market at any price. There may be 5,900,900 acres under rent, and as much more which has been segregated into farms, great and small, preparatory to future cultivation.

This immense breadth of unoccupied land is theoretically open to settlement. But if the state had offered premium for the most effective method of embracing nothing could have been better devised than the system, or rather lack of system, which has obtained here for the last ten years. School bonds, government preemptions, railroad reservations and floating Mexican grants, have made up the tangled skein which is now being slowly unravelled. The attempt made in the last legislature to revive Mexican grant claims, which are about to expire by limitation, was promptly defeated. Even the authors of the scheme have been kept as much in the background as possible. Upon the whole, good many sources of former embarrassment in land titles have ceased to be effective during the last three years. It is easier to ascertain the condition of land title than ever before; and settler with ordinary prudence need not now buy bad title. There is not great breadth of desirable public land now open to preemption. But land can be bought second hand, often at a small advance on government prices. And many persons prefer to pay higher prices and avoid the trouble of perfecting a title from the government.

There is no danger that the lands of this state will be exhausted in years to come even by greatly-increased current of immigration. Most of those who are coming to seek homes want only small parcels of land, which will be all the better for the state, seeing that each settler will be sure to make the most of what he obtains. Of course nearly all desirable farming lands have appreciated in price during the past year, and it is hardly possible now to give any accurate schedule of prices. But within a hundred and fifty miles of this city, we hear of very little unimproved land desirable for cultivation in the market, at less than $5 per acre. And taking this as the minimum, and $50 as the maximum price, there is a large quantity of good land still on the market, and accessible to immigrants. The further the settler goes from markets the cheaper he will get his land. While the markets every year will come nearer to him. The counties of Stanislaus, Merced, Fresno, Tulare, San Luis Obispo, San Bernardino, Santa Barbara and San Diego contain an immense breadth of unoccupied land; and in the last named county parcels have been sold during the present year suitable for stock ranges, at less than the government price.

There is land enough in this state for all who will be likely to seek it for settlement during the next quarter of a century. With an area of 154,216 square miles, there will be elbow room enough even when we have gained an additional population, and now that it is coming, we can at least assure these inquiring thousands that there is room for them, with prospect of as much good fortune as anywhere waits upon honest industry.

shapeless masses.

From Guayaquil, under date of
August 10th, we have brief accounts
of the earthquake in Ecuador.

In the city of Guayaquil, little
damage was done. Ibarra, capital of
the province of Imbabura, San Pablo
and Alturtaqui are in ruins. The en-
tire population of those towns and of
Otovato perished, amounting to near-
ly 10,000.

At Quito the earthquake com-
menced at twenty minutes past 1
o'clock A. M., August 16, and con-
tinued at intervals for few hours.
Up to the last date, the 10th, the
churches, public buildings and private
dwellings were already in ruins, and
the people living in tents in the great
squares.

The towns adjoining Quito, named
Verusho, Puellero and Cochuquanjo,
have almost entirely disappeared,
with their inhabitants.

A Valparaiso letter, dated August
11, says advices from Talquahano,
state that at 9 o'clock, on the night
of August 14, three earthquakes oc-
curred. The second caused an im-
mense tidal wave, which swept away
nearly one-half of the town, and rem-
dered the other half almost unin-
habitable. Four lives only were
lost, the inhabitants fleeing to the
hills.

At Tome the same occurred; but,
being high, little damage was done.
Cobija, Merillones Island, Pissuua,
and all the cities and towns; in fact,
from Cape Francisco, in Ecuador, to
Magellan Straits, suffered more or
less from the terrible visitations of
the earthquake.

At Callao the sea burst over a line
of houses, skirting the shore, at 10
o'clock P. M., on the 18th, com-
pletely cutting them off their contents.
Several vessels collided. No damage
was then done, nearly all putting to
sea. The next night fire broke
out, and fifty-seven houses in the
business portion of the place were
destroyed, entailing a loss of a
$81,500. 900 lives were lost.
The Chincha Islands felt the earth-
quake and wave, but not seriously as
yet known.

The steamer Santiago, bound from
Callao to Valparaiso, put in port off
Chala, when, on the 18th, she was
seized by the great wave, her chains
snapped, and the vessel carried to
sea. In a few minutes the wave re-
turned towards shore, carrying the
steamer with it, and carrying it with
all her passengers safely over a high
cliff, leaving it safely inside the chan-
nel, in the port of Chala, completely
covered with water.

At Caldera the wave and earth-
quake completely destroyed every-
thing, former dwellings being lost.

nure, will produce good bloom of
roses; yet it is always better to put
good shovelful of well rotted ma-
nure into the hole at the time of
planting. Among the evils arising
from planting the rose in poor soil,
is that it frequently makes the flow-
er come single or semi double, so as
to destroy all identity of the variety
by means of its bloom. As gen-
eral principle, it may be laid down
that the rose requires rich soil, and,
if we do not possess that, we must
change the nature of the soil by the
addition of loam, and well rotted
manure.


Some rose culturists take up the
plants every second year for the
purpose of renewing the beds by
deep tillage, and the introduction
of fresh soil in the shape of decayed
turf, muck, leaf-mould, the remains
of old hot beds, etc. When the
plants stand far enough apart, soil
and manure can be added without
disturbing them. Roses of every
kind should be protected by a cov-
ering of some kind from the rigors
of winter. Climbing roses should
be taken down carefully from walls,
arbors and trellises, laid on the
ground, and then covered with dead
leaves, straw or any light littery
substance that will keep them from
exposure to the sun.


Roses should be pruned before
they are covered for the Winter; in
reforming this all dead or decayed
wood should be cut out, and the
young shoots of the last season, cut
back to within three or four inches

exist they shall be laid, by twist-

without breaking. Some persons
make a split with knife at the
place where the layers are to be
placed in the earth, and insert a
thin wedge of wood in the longitu-
dinal cut, to keep it open. This
causes roots to form in short time.

An ordinance relating TO the Bonded Indebtedness OF the city of Davenport.

Whereas, the General Assembly Of the State of Iowa passed an act which was approved Apr 10, 1865, being chapter 81 Of the laws Of the 18th General ASSEMBLY, entitled AN act TO enable Municipal and Public Corporations, at their election TO settle, adjust and compound their indebtedness; and

Whereas, also, the said act gives the city power to pass all ordinances and resolutions necessary TO carry into effect the powers conferred by the said act. Therefore,

BE IT ENACTED by the City Council of the City of Davenport:

Section 1. That as provided by section one and ten of the aforesaid act OF the General Assembly, the question whether the powers given by the said act Of the General Assembly shall be exercised by the City of Davenport, shall be submitted TO the legal voters Of the said city as hereinafter provided. The form Of the question TO be thus submitted, shall be as follows:

Shall the CITY Of Davenport settle its debts under and by virtue Of the provisions OF an act of the General Assembly, entitled AN Act TO enable Municipal and Public Corporations at their election, to settle, adjust and compound their Indebtedness, and to provide for the issue Of new bonds and for the payment Of such new bonds by the levy OF SPECIFIC taxes, and for this purpose altering and amending existing charters and laws, Approved April 10, 1865?

The answer on the ballot containing the question shall be "Yes" or "NO." If the MAJORITY of votes cast are "Yes" then the City Council OF the City of Davenport may IF it finds that satisfactory terms can be had exercise the powers given By the act in the manner therein prescribed and not otherwise, but no officer OF the city can in any event, even IF a majority vote Yes, compel the city TO exercise those powers against its will or against what it deems to be for the best interest Of the city.

Section 2. The vote on the question thus to be submitted shall be taken at special election, to be holden in the city Of Davenport on Saturday, the 18th day Of September, A. D. 1868.

On the said day there shall be polls opened In each ward in the city, A. M. and P. M. and to continue open until 9 o'clock P. M., which said election shall be conducted provided by chapter thirteen of the ordinances Of the city OF Davenport.

The City Council shall appoint judges and clerks for said election who shall qualify according to Law, and who shall canvass the vote and make returns to the City Council required BY the charter and ordinances Of the said city in case Of ordinary municipal elections.

All persons authorized to vote at ordinary city elections are authorized TO vote in the said election herein provided for.

Section 3. A notice of the submission Of said question shall be published in the Davenport Democrat, the Western Islander, and the Radical, or a majority of said papers, for the space of four weeks, to be at least four insertions in said papers, or a majority of them, prior TO the day Of election.

Said notice shall, in substance, notify the electors Of the city that vote will be taken upon the question as set forth in the act by virtue of an act TO enable municipal and public corporations, at their election, to settle, adjust and compound their indebtedness, approved April 10, 1865, and shall be signed BY the City Clerk.

Sec. 4. The result of the election, after being canvassed, shall be entered upon the records OF the city.

Section 5. In case a majority Of the votes cast at said election shall be Yes, all of the restrictions and limitations on the powers Of the commissioners in said act shall be observed By them in making the settlement herein contemplated.

Each Of said Commissioners before entering upon the discharge Of his duties, shall TAKE and subscribe an oath in writing (which shall be preserved BY the City Clerk) as follows:

I, having been appointed Commissioner for the city Of Davenport, under Chapter 81 Of the Laws Of the Twelfth General Assembly, do solemnly swear that I will discharge the duties OF such commissioner to the best OF my ability; that I will observe the provisions of said act and of this ordinance in the discharge of said duties; that I am not the owner, directly or indirectly, of any bonds against the city, nor will I become the owner or interested in any such bonds during the time I shall serve as such Commissioner; and that nothing touching my said appointment shall be in any single to the good of the City.

Each Of said Commissioners appointed by the City Council shall receive full compensation Of all services rendered (except actual expenses and outlays) not to exceed the sum of one hundred dollars per annum, or so long as he shall serve less or more than a year.

Section 6. The commissioners shall exercise the powers given BY the said chapter of the Laws of the Twelfth General Assembly, and the Mayor of the city shall be ex-officio member of the SAID board of Commissioners.

In case the contingency happens in which said Commissioners are TO act, they shall provide a book and keep therein a record of all of their acts and doings; shall keep and preserve all letters addressed TO them or either Of them, and shall retain copies Of letters written to them or either of them in relation to the city debt, all of which shall be subject TO inspection BY order of the Council, and their said record at all times open to public inspection.

And it is hereby declared that no act Of the Board of Commissioners in settling or compromising any debt shall bind the city until such act is reported to the City Council and approved by it.

The City Council shall likewise keep a record of its acts and doings on the premises, which shall also at all times be open to public inspection, and shall be published with the other acts and doings of the City Council.

When President Johnson rose to speak ex-
volunteer General McCook took a standing
position precisely between the President and
the seat assigned to your correspondent.
I politely requested McCook to be seated in a
vacant chair in which he was resting his foot,
and he refused to comply. Mr. Owen Thorn,
one of the managers of the banquet, happen-
ing to pass at that moment, called his atten-
tion to the rudeness of McCook and requested
that he be ordered down so as not to obstruct
the view of the correspondents. Mr. Thorn,
who had special charge of the correspondents'
tables, comprehending the situation, politely
requested McCook to be seated, stating his
reasons for making the request, but he persis-
ted in his exhibition of bad manners, and your
correspondent again turned his attention to
the President, thinking no more of the mat-
ter. He regrets to see announced in the eve-
ning papers personal rencontre between the
gentlemen named, during which blows passed.
I make this explanation as a matter of jus-
tice to Mr. Thorn, who did but his duty on the
occasion and did it in the politest manner pos-
sible,—and at the special request of the corres-
pondent of the Boston Post.

PROVIDENCE, RHODE ISLAND, - -
August, 31st, 1868.


DEAR SIR,—In my previous communications, I
have endeavored to give you faithful account
of the condition of affairs in the East, and the
prospects for the success of the Democratic party
in the Fall Elections. Since my last, I think the
prospect more encouraging than ever. People
are beginning to open their eyes to their own in
terests and cannot, from sheer necessity, support
a Government which requires such stupendous
amount of money to carry out its pernicious de-
signs against an oppressed and down-trodden
section of our common country. The immense
amounts of money which has been collected by
the Government since the close of the war, and
squandered by Government officials without de-
creasing one dollar from the National Debt but
rather increasing said debt, has had the effect of
forcing the masses to think seriously and see
plainly to what state and condition the country
must be brought, if the Radicals are thus allowed
to continue their successes upon the people in
their attempt to organize this &c "Great White
Man's Country." Why, dear Sir, more than a
hundred millions of Dollars have been collected
in Taxes since the close of war—one-half fills
the national debt, and that debt is greater today
than it was three years ago. The South, though poor,
has borne her share of this terrible taxation.
The North, ladened with plenty, has borne by far
the greater portion of it and now is at this
stage. The war has never ended, although
the war has never ended. ALTHOUGH the South laid down
her arms, although her gallant sons returned to-
their desolate homes to change their swords into
plowshares; and their spears into pruning hooks,
Radical hostilities have not ceased. The fight still
continues against over eight millions of men,
women and children with cruelty, oppression and
tyranny and it has cost the country its peace.

Look at the corrupted LEGISLATURE, itself of our
own State whose Halls were once honoured by the
presence of such noble men as Gregg, Butler,
Hampton, Aldrich, and others. Now these places
are filled by thieves and charlatans—thrown in
there as a "war measure"—to riffe the pockets of the
already poverty-stricken people, and to
hold the iron rod of despotism and of tyranny
over their heads. Look at the large standing
army in the South, put there for no other purpose
under heaven than to force upon the people Ne-
gro legislation, Negro judges, such as Platt,
Negro Governors, and Negro Governments. The money goes to them.

And the very best Democratic movement of the
age was made by Congress—at its late session
that was, they voted to continue this system of
Robbery another year. "I glory in their spunk,
but doubt their judgment." The hoax of
"nigger rights and equality" is about "played
out" and the people up there are beginning to see
that they have rights as well as the nigger. Freed
men's Bureaus for negroes have been rather expensive for few years past, and the
people are going to make them use their old fash-
ioned pine tables, and timetables won't have any
napkins on them either.

The people are watching with great alarm
the Government expenditures, and every dollar thus
received comes from their pockets.

About the time the war [started in] Kentucky, [he was] taking me along with him. I forgot to say that I have been told that when I was six weeks old my mother was sold to some planter beyond the Blue Ridge Mountains, and that I never saw her afterward. Many more than a quorum being present,
the Board of Trustees is organized, and will
proceed to business. I deem it useless to
attempt to enforce upon this Board the great
importance of this, the first regular annual
meeting of the Trustees of the University.
The duties of the Board are appreciated, I
doubt not, by all, and the condition of the
University is well known to all the members
of the Board. There is a mortgage upon
the grounds and the buildings of the Uni-
versity to the amount of some $50,900, and
the impression of those who are well in-
formed in regard to the value of the property
is that the grounds, the buildings and the li-
brary are worth at least $150,000 in currency.
The Executive Committee of the Board of
Trustees, in the absence of the Board, have
confined themselves simply to protecting
and guarding the property. We have in-
curred some unavoidable expense, and have
also taken steps to rent out the property of
the University; first to continue to make
good their claims to everything there, and
secondly to aid in defraying expenses. It
will be for the Board to decide in this emer-
gency what shall be asked of the Legisla-
ture. I believe the general wish and the
best interests of all the people of the State
comport with the idea of commencing anew,
as soon as possible and on a larger basis, the
operations of the University.


R. L. Lassiter, Secretary and Treasurer,
read report reviewing at length the condi-
tion of the University, from which it appear-
ed that the Institution is in debt to the
amount of about $100,000, distributed nearly
as follows: The University owned about 100
shares in the stocks of the Bank of North
Carolina, for which it owed that bank $50,
900. The bank has failed, and that debt has
been compromised by agreeing to pay $25,000
in gold. The gold with the premium and
interest is estimated at $4,000 in currency.
There is due Miss Mildred Cameron about
$4,000; to Gov. Swan's estate $4,000; on un-
paid salaries of professors some $1,000; interest
and minor items $4,000. There is also a
claim being pressed in Chowan county by a
woman claiming to be the heir of one Gio-
vanni, Portuguese. That claim, if recover-
ed, will cost the University some $1,000
without interest. There are debts due the
University to the amount of some $40,600,
most of it against insolvent persons or pay-
able in Confederate money, for which little
or nothing will be realized.


The report was accepted and two hundred
copies ordered to be printed.


Mr. Taylor moved that the Legislature be
memorialized to appropriate sum suffi-
cient to lift the indebtedness.


Judge Pearson did not want to ask the
Legislature for money, because the people
are opposed to further taxation to support
the University, unless it was shown upon
what grounds it stood. He moved that the
Chair appoint committee to investigate
the true condition of the finances and report
at the next meeting of the Board.
After some discussion Mr. Cantwell offered
the following resolutions as substitute for
the motions already made:


Resolved, 1st, That a committee of three
be appointed by the chair to inquire into
and report upon the legality of the debt
secured by the deed of trust of the Bank,
April 1867, and also all other debts claim-
ed to be due by the University, with authori-
ty to employ counsel and to send for person-
s and papers.


Resolved, 2d, That a committee of three
be appointed by the chair to memorialize
the honorable the General Assembly for
a sum of money sufficient to cover the expen-
ses of resuming the exercises at the Univer-
sity at the earliest practicable moment.


The resolutions were adopted, and the
President appointed, under the first resol-
ution, Messrs Edward Cantwell, E. G. Reade,
and A. W. Tourgee; and under the sec-
ond resolution he appointed W. B. Rodman,
S. Ashley and Solomon Pool.


On motion of Mr. Cantwell the first com-
mittee was instructed to report at the ne-
xt meeting of the Board. The order to pri-
nt the Secretary and Treasurer's report was
rescinded in order to print with it this re-
port when received.


The Board adjourned until Wednesday
three o'clock, P. M.

CHICAGO, June 10, 1868. -
To the Editor of The Illinois Statesman:

Dr. Wise, the editor of the Israelite, published at Cincinnati, has, in his own estimation, the merit, but in mine, the heavy responsibility of adding an Israelitic question to the many other party issues which are now convulsing our republic. He declares that in view of the well-known General Order No. 11, no Israelite of honor or self-respect can or should vote for Grant. The Democratic papers of the country were naturally prompt to make capital out of this, and we shall see this subject well worked out by all the Democratic stump orators up to the time of the election. To the best of my knowledge but few replies from Israelites have appeared in Republican papers and those treated the subject very tenderly. The public at large would, therefore, naturally believe that there was such a question as "Grant and the Israelites."

I was much pleased to see in your paper of yesterday, that my friend Doctor Chronik had, on your invitation, expressed his views upon the matter. I thought at first that he would make a true statement without ifs or butts. But I found that I was deceived, and laid the paper on one side. I found his answer much like milk and water seasoned with wormwood. Now, if you have the space, sir, I am prepared to give you the more clear and more definite opinion of an Israelite.

There is no such question as Grant and the Israelites. There is but one question, and that is "Grant and the Democrats." It is a mere deception when Israelitic Democrats bear before them the Israelitic flag. I am a Jew, when Saturday, the seventh day, comes; I am one in my dietary, in the selection and treatment of my food; it is always written on my door-posts, it is always spoken in my prayers, and it is always to be seen in my reverence for my Bible, that I am a Jew. I fast on the day of the destruction of Jerusalem, and mourn that catastrophe which befell my ancestors. But it is different when I take a ballot in order to exercise my rights as a citizen. Then I am not a Jew, but I feel and act as a citizen of the republic. I do not ask what pleases the Israelites, I consult the welfare of the country, if that party in whose hands I believed the welfare of the country, so far as the advancement of human rights was concerned, was the safest. We're to place Haman at the helm of State, and if the opposite party, whose non-existence I believed would be better for humanity and my country, were to place Messiah at their head, Moses the Chief Justice, and call the patriarchs into the Cabinet, I should say: "Prosper under Haman, my father," and here you have my vote, even if all the Jew in me mourned.

Such a view of the case is not anti-Judaic. The Babylonians overthrew the Jewish Kingdom, destroyed the city and burned the Temple, and the ruins were yet smoking with the blood that had been shed when Jeremiah called out to the refugees, "Pray for Babylon and seek her welfare, since from now on Babylon's welfare is your welfare." The welfare of the United States is our welfare. If Grant is the best man for the Americans he is the best man for us Israelites, despite General Order No. 11.

But I am far from holding Grant for an enemy of the Jews. To-day no educated man is an enemy of the Jews. If Grant had in quiet and peaceful times, officially or privately, expressed himself concerning the Jews after the fashion of General Order No. 11, this susceptibility would do well. If any one insults or treats me, I do not take it quietly like a sheep. But when my own house burns and the fire marshal, in whose way I am standing, in his eagerness to extinguish it, strikes me over the head or in the ribs so as to knock me across the street, I do not take it ill.

BOTS IN HORSES—It is a prevalent impression that bots often cause the death of horses. This conclusion is discredited by DR. Stewart, in the American Farmers Horse Book. His opinion is that the true character of the bot and its influence on the health of the horse have been misunderstood very generally; that the bot is hereditary with the horse, and found attached by the tail to the coating of the stomach of the colt in the shape of a parasite. In this normal condition the bot causes no injury to the horse, has no relationship to the grub or worm, the last being the offspring of the gad lily, which deposits its eggs upon the hair of the horse and are bitten off and swallowed by the animal. These develop into worms in time; pass on with the excrement, burrow in the ground, where chrysalis is formed and in time succession of gad flies is the result. This grub, unlike the bot, never attaches itself to the coating of the stomach but amid the food the same as worms in the stomach of child. These worms may cause much uneasiness to the horse but never death.

As to the bot and his operations, DR. Stewart adds:—"The cutaneous coating of the stomach to which the bot fastens himself by means of two little bearded hooks, is nearly, if not wholly, insensible, having more feeling apparently than the animal's boots. When the nose is in health it is hard, rigid, impenetrable, and the bot, if ever so much disposed to do so, would attack it in vain; but when death seizes him this coating becomes relaxed and soft, and begins rapidly to decompose. Then only is it that the bot can or ever does work his way through it. Another fact still more strong corroborative of the above proposition, is this: that of any number of horses killed while in perfect health, and opened an hour or two afterward, there will be found not one whose stomach is not riddled by the bot. Dissection has revealed the existence of this condition in hundreds of instances of sudden death from accident.

This kidding of the stomach is consequence not the cause of the death of the horse, according to the theory here presented. When the animal dies from the effects of disease or from accidental causes the instinct of the bot teaches it that decomposition of its home, the stomach of the horse, must readily take place, involving its own death, hence its prompt efforts to escape from its fostering prison. It is the same instinct which induces rats to attempt escape from a sinking ship or from building threatened with destruction by fire or submersion by water. If this is the true solution of the bot question, the care of the horse will be considerably simplified and ailing animals relieved from many disagreeable drenchings designed to expel from their stomach what has been generally regarded a mortal enemy. Those well posted in regard to the horse his enemies and diseases, will doubtless give the theory of DR. Stewart, in reference to the bot proper consideration.

CURE FOR FOUNDER.—The Rural World proposes to cure founder in horses in this way: Take the horse into a brook stream of water deep enough to nearly reach his body, and stand him there with his head so high that he cannot drink. If the weather is warm keep him there several hours. Then remove him and rub his LEGS thoroughly to promote circulation. If it is lame repeat the process two three times and cure will be effected. In the winter twenty minutes will be long enough to keep the horse in the water when he should be taken out and rubbed as in the other case repeating the operation. Grafton Unnecessary. This is said to cure all cases of founder, when not of long standing.

It launches out into a recapitulation of its own
doughty achievements, and hints that if the
State hath hearkened to its counsel the Club
House Convention would never have been held.
It alludes to its appeals to the constitution,
and finally—with a great tipping of wings—
crows that the policy of the Mercury has been
adopted by the whole country, and that the
whole of the United States are, in fact, no
thing more than the tin kettle which clatters
at the heels of the Mercury, as it runs up and
down every lane and alley of the great thing as it
has been.

All this is a good joke, but we submit to our
contemporary that this warm weather is hardly
a fit time to kill one with laughter. Of course,
it is admitted that the Mercury is a very decent
average newspaper, but when it leaps at one
bound into the heavens of biggest circulation,
it must expect to be taken at its word and chal-
lenged to the proof.

The Mercury says: "We have now no
hesitation in saying that we have the larg-
est number of permanent annual and semi-
annual subscribers of any journal in South
Carolina." This is very foggy. What does
it mean? Does it mean that the Mercury has
a larger daily circulation than any other paper
in South Carolina? If so, it had better not try
to count chips with The Charleston Daily
News. Again what does it mean by bona
fide circulation? The News understands a bona
fide circulation to be—the number of
copies issued daily for cash, or to sub-
scribers who have paid in advance, accord-
ing to the published terms of the Charleston
News. If this be the way our funny
neighbor understands it, The News denies.

MYSTERIOUS Transaction—Murder

Attack Upon Young Lady

From the Detroit Tribune, October 9.

At the present time citizens living in the immediate vicinity of the corner of Michigan avenue and Sixth street are greatly agitated lest a murder and possibly other terrible crimes shall be committed. While one family is the most excited over the matter, the feeling of insecurity is prevalent through the entire neighborhood. On Monday night last a bold and outrageous attempt was made to murder a young lady named Mary Sanford, residing with the family of Mr. Deering, who is the proprietor of a dry goods store on the corner above named. She was met by some man at or near the corner of Eighth and Fort streets, early in the evening, and came very near losing her life. The wretch, whoever he was, made three separate attempts to stab the young lady, and cut her hat in as many places, appearances would indicate, with a razor.

Several days since an anonymous note was sent to the house of Mr. Deering for Miss Sanford, in which the writer requested a private interview with her, concerning matters which the person said interested her only. The writer selected a certain locality and time for the meeting. Mr. Deering accompanied the young lady, but as nothing could be seen of the mysterious personage at the appointed place, they returned home. Another note was then sent, which stated that the writer wished to see Miss Sanford alone, and appointed Monday evening as the time and the corner of Eighth and Fort streets as the place of meeting. On this occasion Mr. Deering remained at home, and another gentleman went as an escort with Miss Sanford. As they neared the locality last referred to, the gentleman walked down one side of Eighth street, the better to observe any movements that might be made, while she walked on the other side of the street. As she approached a secluded spot near Richardson's match factory, an unknown man jumped from near the fence and struck the young lady a powerful blow upon the head. She immediately cried for assistance, and the gentleman who had accompanied her, as a guard, rushed to her assistance. Before he could reach her, however, the would-be murderer had dealt her two other blows, and, observing that he was in danger of being captured, fled toward Lafayette avenue. He was hotly pursued, and every possible effort made, but in vain, to capture him. Miss Sanford was found not to have been seriously injured, and was escorted back to Mr. Deering's residence. Her hat and the anonymous letters are now in the possession of the police detectives, who are endeavoring to ferret out the assassin. We regret to state, however, that the chances for arresting the scoundrel are not good. The attack was made so suddenly that Miss Sanford had no opportunity to see the face of the party, nor even fair chance to notice the kind of color of his clothing.

Since this event several letters have been sent to Mr. Deering's residence, all of a threatening nature, but by whom they were written, or for what cause, remains a mystery, which the future can only solve. There is entertained one solution to the attempted murder, but this may or may not be correct. The statement was made to us by Mr. Deering, and we give it substantially as related by Miss Sanford: her parents formerly lived at Lyons, Clinton county, Iowa, and were quite wealthy; a brother of her father and his wife lived in New Orleans, Louisiana, and the family of the former—Mary being the only daughter—went to New Orleans to pay a visit to their relatives there. Miss Sanford was then quite young. She is now sixteen years of age. While at New Orleans her father and mother were stricken down with yellow fever and died there. Her uncle and aunt subsequently moved North and took possession of the Sanford estate at Lyons, Iowa. They cared for Mary as relations should and lived in comfort and ease upon the fortune of her deceased father. Mary always passed as and was known as the daughter of the surviving Sanford, until very recently, when the facts were made known to her that she was living with her uncle, that her father was dead, and that the property that she supposed belonged to her uncle was really her property. These things were made so clear to her that she could not fail to understand them and she began to assert her rights under the circumstances. At that time she was regarded by her relatives as a dangerous person to have about the premises. Grievances, real or supposed, it matters not, came thick and fast, and Miss Sanford, having previously formed the acquaintance of the Deering family—who were then engaged in the dry goods and millinery business at Lyons, Iowa—was afforded shelter by them. WASHINGTON, Dec. 19.—Correspondence of the Boston Post.

The assassination announced the murder of Reno and Charles Anderson by a mob at New Albany, Ind., has occasioned great excitement in official circles. Were the honor of the government had been pledged to the Canadian authorities for the protection of these men and of their safe return to Canada, if not convicted after trial on the charge of robbing Adams Express, it was only after this pledge had been given that these men were surrendered to the United States under the provisions of the extradition treaty. all the clouds that lowered o'er our house are
deep in the bosom of the ocean buried" by this
son of New York, who has come to me. I think
I love him, and think I do not.


Every heart has its silent hour, and so has
mine."—Camille Aux.


Nay the 2nd.—I am still the same. There are
others still the same. He has been to see me
to-day, and he says he loves me. am still a
woman, and feel that I love him. I sung him,
and being tired, retired. Bonne nuit—which is
what it means without day specified!


Nay 3rd.—To-day went with He to the
theater, because the theater couldn't come to us.

loved me. I don't blame him, for I love myself.

esteem was as large as my waterfall. In the
words of the poet:

June (not "Jennie") June—have read the

there is Wife Wanted—" I am not a wife, so

When woman says she will, she will;

When woman says she WON'T she won't, and

18th, gave the following portraits of

our wounded, as it is proven by many

eted by this rebel chief as they lay
